documents: Zhao, Guo & Wang (2022), Asthenospheric flow from East Asia to the Philippine Sea Plate revealed by rj-MCMC inversion of surface waves, Geochemistry, Geophysics, Geosystems 23, e2022GC010342: published PDF, 17 pp. (Supporting Information S1 not supplied)
pages_convention: PDF pages counted from 1 (identical to the printed article pages 'n of 17')

entry.evidence: The formation of widely distributed intraplate volcanoes and the dynamic pattern of the entire region are still debated.

steps.action: The authors pose the open questions: the origin of the intraplate volcanism in NE Asia (especially around the Korean Peninsula), and how plate interactions control mantle flow (pp. 1-2).
steps.quote: The formation of widely distributed intraplate volcanoes and the dynamic pattern of the entire region are still debated.

steps.action: They list published rival dynamic models for intraplate volcanism: wet upwelling from the stagnant slab, return flow at the slab edge, escape of hot material through a slab gap, and sub-lithospheric convection.
steps.quote: numerous dynamic models have been proposed to account for the formation of intraplate volcanism in NE Asia

steps.action: They cite published shear-wave splitting studies that show complex anisotropy, and note that the limited depth sensitivity and sparse stations of these studies restrict 3-D flow interpretation.
steps.quote: the limited depth sensitivity of anisotropy due to the nearly vertical incidence of teleseismic SKS waves

steps.action: They build a modified transdimensional rj-MCMC inversion for azimuthally anisotropic Rayleigh-wave dispersion, with a depth-varying layered prior on Vsv to reduce trade-offs and non-uniqueness. Details: forward kernels from CPS, priors from AK135 and CRUST1.0, a fixed data-noise model, an error-transfer formula for uncertainties, and modified acceptance ratios in Appendix A (pp. 4-7, 13-15).
steps.quote: we presented a modified rj-MCMC method for inversion of azimuthally anisotropic surface wave dispersion

steps.action: They take as input the 2-D anisotropic Rayleigh phase-velocity maps (15-150 s, 40 km grid, 66 stations) published by Fan et al. (2020).
steps.quote: we use azimuthally anisotropic Rayleigh wave dispersion data from a recent surface wave tomography dataset

steps.action: They invert each grid node for 1-D posterior PDFs and assemble the posterior mean models into a 3-D isotropic and azimuthally anisotropic Vsv model. Data fits are shown in Figures 2d-2f and 4, and posterior PDFs in Figure 3.
steps.quote: We obtained the 3-D anisotropic shear wave velocity structure of NE Asia by assembling all one-dimensional (1-D) posterior mean models

steps.action: Because the posterior widens below about 200 km, they restrict interpretation to the uppermost mantle (200 km or shallower).
steps.quote: Thus, the discussion was only focused on the uppermost mantle structure (≤200 km).

steps.action: They rerun the sampler with five chains and compare the result with the single-chain posterior; the two are highly consistent (Figures S2-S3).
steps.quote: we also compared results from 1 chain and 5 chains

steps.action: They read the depth slices: low velocities beneath volcanoes and rift basins, high-velocity anomalies HV1 and HV2, rotating fast directions, and Japan Sea anisotropy parallel to spreading. They report posterior uncertainties (Figure S4: Vsv uncertainty mostly below 150 m/s, larger at the margins) (pp. 8-10).
steps.quote: Two significant high-velocity anomalies were found beneath the southern Songliao Basin and the central Korean Peninsula

steps.action: They set their finger-like shallow low-velocity bodies beneath the CBV, CRV and ULV against the large-scale deep upwelling seen in body-wave tomography, and infer localized asthenospheric upwellings feeding the volcanoes.
steps.quote: which suggests that localized asthenospheric upwellings feed these intraplate volcanoes

steps.action: They adopt the explanation of Song et al. (2020) that HV2 beneath the central Korean Peninsula is a Rayleigh-Taylor lithospheric drip of a preserved cratonic root.
steps.quote: this anomaly represents the Rayleigh-Taylor-type lithospheric drip of the remaining cratonic root

steps.action: They use published body-wave tomography to extend the drip below the depth resolved by surface waves.
steps.quote: a recent body wave tomographic image reveals that the lithospheric drip does extend down to a depth of over 240 km

steps.action: They cite numerical modelling that predicts lithospheric downwelling controls localized upwelling and volcanism around it.
steps.quote: Numerical modeling has predicted that the downwelling of the lithosphere may control the localized asthenospheric upwelling

steps.action: They compare this prediction with their model: low-velocity anomalies surround HV2, especially beneath Halla volcano. They propose that the drip controls the distribution of volcanoes around the Korean Peninsula.
steps.quote: we also found localized low-velocity anomalies surrounding the HV2, particularly beneath the HLV

steps.action: They relate the trench-perpendicular NWW-SEE fast direction above 100 km to absolute plate motion (GSRM v2.1), Pacific slab retreat and the opening of the Japan Sea.
steps.quote: This trench-perpendicular anisotropy is likely to be related to the retreat of the Pacific Plate and the opening of the Japan Sea

steps.action: Synthetic tests (Figures S5-S6) check that the inversion can resolve multilayer anisotropy below 100 km.
steps.quote: Synthetic tests shown in Figures S5 and S6 of Supporting Information S1 verified that such multilayer anisotropy could be resolved by the inversion

steps.action: They forward-compute the SKS splitting delay times and fast directions their 3-D anisotropic model predicts, assuming vertical S-wave propagation.
steps.quote: we computed the delay time and fast direction by assuming that the S-wave vertically propagates through the 3-D anisotropic material

steps.action: They compare the predicted splitting with an independent compilation of observed SWS measurements (Figure 7a); the orientations match over most of the land area.
steps.quote: the pattern of SWS orientations matches well with the prediction from our anisotropy model beneath most of the study area on land

steps.action: They attribute the underestimated predicted delay times to an auxiliary: Fan et al. resolution tests show that tomography underestimates anisotropy amplitude by over 50%. The anisotropy model is not revised.
steps.quote: the predicted delay time is underestimated overall in comparison with the observed splitting

steps.action: They set the clockwise rotation of the fast direction toward the Nankai Trough against published evidence for a slab window: slab segmentation (Wu et al. 2016), the absence of a fast slab in GAP-P4, and a lack of intermediate-depth seismicity in the USGS catalog (Figure 7b) (pp. 12-13).
steps.quote: intermediate seismicity indicates that the slab window has a length of the order of 300 km at depths of 90–250 km

steps.action: They propose that mantle flows from East China to the Philippine Sea Plate through the Nankai slab window, drawn by spreading in the Mariana Trough.
steps.quote: [...] that the clockwise rotation of the fast direction beneath NE Asia may indicate mantle flow from East China to the Philippine Sea Plate

steps.action: They keep the claim that at least part of the eastward asthenospheric flow from East China enters the Philippine Sea Plate through the [...] , and restate it in the Conclusion.
steps.quote: Our study suggests that at least part of the eastward asthenospheric materials from East China do flow into the Philippine Sea Plate

tree.answer: Yes: widespread intraplate volcanism far from the trench, and debated mantle flow beneath NE Asia
No: mantle structure and flow are inferred from surface-wave dispersion through a forward model
Estimate a 3-D anisotropic Vsv model and interpret it in terms of mantle dynamics
Rival models are cited (wet upwelling, return flow, slab gap, small-scale convection; contested destination of the eastward flow) but not tested one against another
No distinct predictions of the rivals are derived
Conditions are found: present-day mantle structure imaged from existing data
Partly: the chains agree, synthetic tests resolve multilayer anisotropy, and SWS orientations match, but predicted delay times are too small
Flow through the Nankai slab window is suggested as the interpretation consistent with the anisotropy, tomography and seismicity

end.claim: The clockwise rotation of fast directions beneath NE Asia toward the Nankai Trough indicates that at least part of the eastward asthenospheric flow from East China passes into the Philippine Sea Plate through the [...] .

decisive_move.sentence: The rj-MCMC inversion of the Fan et al. (2020) dispersion data into a 3-D anisotropic Vsv model produced the clockwise fast-direction rotation, the localized low-velocity bodies and HV2, on which every interpretive claim rests.

gates.evidence: Action: the data are published phase-velocity maps (Fan et al., 2020), not acquired under a hypothesis (p. 4). Claim: the model faced an independent check against SWS observations that it could have failed, and the orientations matched while delay times did not (p. 12). The mantle-flow and drip interpretations face no test that could fail and are framed as 'suggest' or 'plausible' (pp. 11, 13). Registration: priors were set from AK135 and CRUST1.0 before the inversion, but no hypothesis, analysis or threshold was fixed before the data were seen; the anisotropic data uncertainty was set 'according to some tests' (p. 7).

imports.item: Reversible-jump (transdimensional) Markov chain Monte Carlo and Bayesian model determination (Green 1995, 2003)

novelty_claims.quote: we presented a modified rj-MCMC method for inversion of azimuthally anisotropic surface wave dispersion
Findings of this study can be expected to form a new theoretical basis for the formation and spatial distribution of Cenozoic volcanoes

limits: Sub-claims and their statuses: the 3-D anisotropic Vsv model (0-200 km) is estimate_with_resolution, with posterior uncertainties (Figure S4) and lateral resolution inherited from Fan et al. checkerboard tests. Localized upwellings beneath volcanoes and HV2 as a lithospheric drip are best_explanation; the drip is called 'one plausible explanation', its depth rests on Song et al. (2020), and its control on volcano distribution is 'possible'. The modified rj-MCMC is capability_characterized only through chain agreement and synthetic tests in a supplement that was not supplied. The supplementary figures (S1-S6) were not available to this coder, so the V checks are coded from main-text statements. No alternative interpretation of the clockwise rotation is stated or excluded (for example, frozen lithospheric fabric, or flow around the stagnant slab), so the headline claim is coded best_explanation against an implicit field of rivals, not a stated one. The underestimated delay times are absorbed by an auxiliary (amplitude underestimation in the input tomography) rather than tested. The effect of the layered prior relative to a uniform prior is asserted, not shown. Composition coded none_fits (inference): the walk is estimation from existing data followed by post hoc synthesis with published tomography and seismicity, with no crucial test and no repeated independent traces, so it is neither strong_inference nor a clean trace_series. No review file was supplied, so question 9 is unanswered and there is no review sequence.

disagreements.support: The higher-resolution surface-wave model shows finger-like localized low-velocity bodies in the uppermost mantle beneath individual volcanoes, rather than one broad upwelling.
disagreements.quote: showed finger-like low-velocity bodies in the uppermost mantle beneath active volcanoes

disagreements.target: Significant Mesozoic craton modification of the central Korean Peninsula (Gao et al. 2008; Zheng et al. 2011; Zhu et al. [...]
disagreements.support: The cylinder-shaped fast anomaly HV2, extending to at least 150 km, is read as a locally preserved thick cratonic root now dripping.
disagreements.quote: [...] could be that the thick cratonic lithosphere was locally preserved during the Mesozoic craton destruction

disagreements.target: Contested destination of the eastward mantle flow beneath eastern China (Jolivet et al. 2018; S. Li et al. 2020; Schellart [...]
disagreements.support: Fast directions rotating toward the Nankai Trough, together with slab-window evidence from tomography and seismicity, are taken to show that at least part of the flow enters the Philippine Sea Plate.
disagreements.quote: although the destination of the mantle flow is controversial

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Simple uniform prior used in previous rj-MCMC studies
alternatives_considered.reason: Surface waves are less sensitive to discontinuities such as the Moho; a tighter constraint reduces non-uniqueness and improves stability
The posteriors from one and five chains are highly consistent, so one chain is enough

alternatives_considered.chosen: Anisotropic data uncertainty fixed at 2 m/s (about 40% of the mean |a_c,s|)
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Other settings explored in unspecified tests
alternatives_considered.reason: Balance isotropic and anisotropic data, following 'some tests and previous practices' (Yao 2015)
